branches.title: What to pack
branches.sub: Tick it off as it goes in the case
branches.lead: Tick it off as it goes in the case. It saves itself, so you can come back to it.

items.t: Two iḥrām sheets, and a spare set
items.d: One set gets wet, sandy or stained within a day or two. A spare is the difference between washing in a hotel sink at midnight and not.

art.cap: A cotton belt with zipped pockets, worn over the izār.

items.d: It holds the sheets and keeps your phone, money and room key on you. Pockets matter: there are none in an iḥrām.
Whether they may be used on an iḥrām is a question for the ʿulamā, not for a packing list. Take them either way; they are useful for everything else.
For women, and for men outside iḥrām. Thin cotton, loose enough for air to move. Black absorbs heat but hides dust; most people take both.
The desert at night in winter is cold, Minā tents are air-conditioned hard, and aeroplanes are freezing. One fleece covers all three.

items.t: A travel wash bar or sachets
items.d: You will be rinsing clothes in a sink. Hotel laundry during the season is slow and expensive.

sections.title: Unscented washing
sections.lead: Scented soap, shampoo, deodorant and toothpaste are the single most common thing people get caught out by. Buy unscented before you fly: it is far easier to find in a British supermarket than in Makkah during the season.

items.d: Check the bottle, not the brand. Many 'sensitive' ranges are still perfumed.
Crystal or plain alum sticks are widely used.
Mint counts as a scent to many; take a plain one and ask the ʿulamā rather than guessing in the hotel.
Lips crack badly in that air. An unscented balm is worth more than it sounds.
Factor 50. Scalps burn in iḥrām with no cap, and the tops of the feet burn in sandals — both are places people forget.
Not unusual there; half the courtyard carries one. It is the best shade you can own and it weighs nothing.
Zamzam coolers are everywhere in the Ḥaram. A bottle you can refill means you drink far more than you otherwise would.
Water alone does not replace what you sweat out. A few sachets weigh nothing and are the quickest way back from feeling wrung out.
Long days, missed meals and heat drop your blood sugar. Something in a pocket for the walk back from Ḥaram is worth carrying.
For the face and the back of the neck while queueing in the sun. Make sure it is unscented water.

sections.title: Feet
sections.lead: More Hajj trips are spoiled by feet than by anything else. You will walk further than you expect, on marble that is polished, hot and unforgiving.

items.t: Sandals you have already worn in
items.d: Never take new ones. Which kind may be worn in iḥrām is a ruling, and it is in the Iḥrām branch; for comfort, take the ones your feet already know.
Shoes go missing outside the Ḥaram constantly. A spare pair in the room means it is an annoyance rather than a crisis.
Carry your sandals in with you. It is the single best tip anybody gives a first-timer.
Treat a hot spot the moment you feel it, not that evening.
Marble is cold at Fajr and scorching by Ẓuhr.

items.t: Your own medication, in its original packaging
items.d: With the pharmacy label on it, and a copy of your prescription or a letter from your GP. Some medicines that are ordinary here are controlled there, so check the official Saudi guidance before you fly rather than hoping.
Pharmacies are everywhere and cheap, but not at three in the morning when you need them.
Dust, crowds and a few million people breathing the same air. Most people come home with a cough; a mask in the crowded parts helps.
Whether alcohol-based sanitiser is a problem in iḥrām is a question for the ʿulamā. Alcohol-free wipes avoid the question.
Different water, different food, eaten at odd hours.
Printed as well as on your phone. Phones die and batteries run out in queues.
One set in your case, one with somebody travelling with you.

items.t: A card with your name, hotel and a contact number
items.d: In Arabic and English, in your iḥrām belt. If you are lost, confused or unwell, this is what gets you home. Take one for every member of your group, especially the elderly.
Check it actually covers Hajj or ʿUmrah; some policies exclude it.

items.t: A card that works abroad, and some riyals
items.d: Cards are accepted widely now, but small stalls, barbers and taxis are easier with cash.
Do not assume the sockets match yours. Take an adapter that covers more than one shape.
You will be out of the room for six hours at a time and navigating, translating and calling the whole while.
Hotel sockets are never near the bed, and rooms are shared.
For Muzdalifah, and for finding your tent at night.

branches.title: Heat, water and crowds
branches.sub: Staying upright in the heat and the crowd
branches.lead: Most of what goes wrong on Hajj is heat, dehydration or a crowd, and all three are survivable if you know what you are looking at.

items.d: By the time you feel thirsty in that heat you are already behind. Drink on a schedule rather than on a feeling: a little, often, all day.

items.t: Zamzam is everywhere in the Ḥaram
items.d: Coolers line the courtyards and the floors. There is never a reason to walk past one thirsty.
You lose salts as well as water. If you feel wrung out, headachy or oddly weak after a long day, a rehydration sachet usually does more than another bottle of water.
Dark urine means drink more. It is unglamorous and it is the most reliable signal you have.

sections.title: When the heat is winning
sections.lead: Learn these, for yourself and for whoever you are travelling with. Older pilgrims often will not say anything.

items.t: Heat exhaustion: get out of the sun now
items.d: Heavy sweating, cold clammy skin, a fast weak pulse, dizziness, cramp, nausea, headache. Move into shade or air conditioning, loosen clothing, sip water with salts, cool the skin. It usually passes within half an hour of doing the right thing.

Hot dry skin or sweating that has STOPPED, a pounding pulse, confusion, slurred speech, fainting. Call for help straight away, get them into shade, and cool them with whatever water you have while you wait. Do not wait to see if it improves.
The elderly, anybody fasting, anybody on blood pressure or water tablets, and anybody too proud to complain. Confusion is the sign people miss, because the person cannot report it themselves.

items.t: Keep the middle of the day quiet
items.d: Ṭawāf and saʿī at Fajr or after ʿIshāʾ are a different experience from the same thing at two in the afternoon. Rest when the sun is highest; the Ḥaram is open all night.

items.t: The marble gets hot enough to burn
items.d: It is cooled in parts of the courtyard and not in others. In sandals, keep to shade and to the cooled strips; a burnt sole ends your walking for days.

items.t: A bare head in iḥrām burns fast
items.d: Sunscreen on the scalp, the ears and the tops of the feet. Use an umbrella. Men cannot cover the head in iḥrām, which makes shade a necessity rather than a comfort.

items.t: Agree a meeting point before you go in
items.d: A gate number, not 'by the door'. Everyone in the group should know it and be able to say it. Phones do not work well in those crowds.

items.t: Move with the crowd, never across it
items.d: If you need to leave, work diagonally towards the edge over time. Turning and pushing back is how people fall.

items.t: Do not fight your way to the Black Stone
items.d: People are hurt there every year. Pointing from a distance as you pass is the practice of the Prophet ﷺ, and nobody is better for an injury.

items.t: If you drop something, leave it
items.d: Bending down in a moving crowd is one of the most dangerous things you can do. A phone is replaceable.

items.t: Never go alone without telling somebody
items.d: Where you are going and roughly when you will be back. Especially at night, and especially in Minā where every tent looks like every other tent.

branches.title: Before you book
branches.sub: What to check before you pay
branches.lead: Entry rules, visas and vaccination requirements change from season to season. What follows is what to go and check, not what the answer is.

sections.title: Check these yourself, close to flying

items.d: Hajj and ʿUmrah are issued differently and through official channels. Use the Saudi government's own route and your tour operator; do not rely on what somebody was told two years ago.

items.t: The ETA — the visa ʿUmrah is travelled on

link.t: Apply on Saudi Arabia’s visa service

items.d:
There is no such thing as an ʿUmrah visa. ʿUmrah is performed on an ordinary visitor visa, and for a British citizen that is the Electronic Travel Authorization — the ETA.

It is a MULTIPLE-ENTRY authorization valid for 730 days, which is two years, and it allows a stay of up to 180 days at a time. It costs 50 Saudi riyals, it is not refundable once issued, and it is usually decided within one to three working days. Everybody travelling needs their own, children included.

The service lists it for tourism, business, study and medical treatment, and its own FAQ answers the question plainly: yes, you may perform ʿUmrah during your stay. It cannot be used for work, and it CANNOT BE USED FOR HAJJ — that is a different visa and a different route entirely.

Those figures were read off the Ministry’s own service in November 2026. They are Saudi Arabia’s to change and this app is not the place to find out they have: check them on the service before you pay.

items.t: The Hajj visa is not applied for the same way
items.d:
A Hajj visa is not something you apply for yourself the way an ʿUmrah one is, and the ETA will not do instead — the Ministry’s own service says in as many words that it cannot be used for Hajj. It comes with a package, and packages for pilgrims travelling from outside the Kingdom are released through Nusuk Hajj on the Saudi ministry’s own schedule — you choose a package there, and the visa follows from it.

So the thing to watch is when packages open, not when a visa form appears. Follow the rules and the package information published with them, because they set the dates, the price and what is included, and they change between seasons.

items.t: Set up Nusuk before you fly

link.t: Get Nusuk on the App Store

items.d: Nusuk is the Saudi ministry’s own app and the permits are issued through it, so install it and get the account working at home rather than in a queue at the other end. The ʿUmrah permit is booked in it. So is the permit for the Rawḍah at the Prophet’s Masjid in Madīnah ﷺ, which is released in timed slots and goes quickly — people who leave that one until they arrive often do not get it.

items.t: Vaccinations, and the certificate you have to show
items.d:
Saudi Arabia sets the vaccination requirements for pilgrims and revises them, so check the current list on the UK’s own travel health service as well as with whoever is vaccinating you. The one actually checked at the border is meningococcal, and a certificate that has expired counts the same as none at all — for Hajj treat it as an entry requirement rather than as advice.

There are two ways to get it. Bolton Council of Mosques’ Health Forum has run a not-for-profit clinic for pilgrims for over twenty years, certificate included and all ages done, booked and paid for IN ADVANCE at 1 Vicarage Street, Bolton BL3 5LE. They run set dates each season rather than on demand, so ring and ask which are open; the current poster puts it at £30 a person, and admin@thebcom.org reaches them too. Or your own GP surgery, which may be simpler if you are registered there.

Either way go early rather than waiting for an appointment to come round: some keep the vaccine in stock and some have to order it, and others on the list need more than one dose or time to take effect. Ask that the certificate says what Saudi Arabia asks it to say — a vaccination recorded in your notes and a certificate you can show at a border are not the same thing.

items.t: The UK's travel advice for Saudi Arabia
items.d: The Foreign Office page is updated through the season and covers entry rules, safety and what the consulate can do if something goes wrong.
Some medicines sold freely here are controlled there. Check the official guidance, carry them in the original packaging, and take your prescription.
Read the exclusions. Several ordinary travel policies will not cover Hajj or ʿUmrah, and medical care abroad is not free.

items.t: Women: check the dates before you pay
items.d: Ṭawāf is done inside the Masjid, and ḥayḍ or nifās stops a woman entering it — so a fixed set of dates can leave an ʿUmrah unfinishable through nobody’s fault. Work out where your dates are likely to fall before the booking is confirmed, and put the question to the ʿulamā at that point rather than on the plane. The iḥrām branch has what they say about it.
People from this community go every year. The office can often tell you which operators others have used and what caught them out, which is worth more than a forum.

branches.title: Iḥrām
branches.sub: What may be worn, and what is owed
branches.lead: What may be worn, what may not be done, and what is owed if something is broken.

art.cap: The izār at the waist and the ridāʾ over the shoulder.

marks.t: The head is uncovered — nothing rests on it.
The ridāʾ, over one shoulder and across the chest, leaving the other shoulder bare.
The izār, wrapped at the waist and held without a belt or a pin.
The hem falls above the ankle, and the feet are bare.

items.d: An izār around the lower body and a ridāʾ over the upper, both unstitched and ordinarily white. Nothing sewn to the shape of the body is worn. Iḥrām in this sense is for men: a woman enters iḥrām without any special garment.

A man in iḥrām covers neither his head nor his face. The line is contact, not shade: an umbrella, a parasol, the roof of a car or a bus is fine so long as it does not rest on the head, while a cap, a towel or a fold of the ridāʾ laid over it is not.

items.t: Footwear that leaves the instep bare

art.cap: A toe post leaves the instep — the raised middle bone — uncovered.
A broad strap covers the instep completely.

items.d: For men, footwear that covers the raised middle bone on top of the foot is not worn. That one bone is the whole test, and it is why a toe-post sandal passes where a broad-strapped one does not.

art.cap: Loose, full length, with the head covered. Nothing in this picture is a special garment.

marks.t: The head and the hair are covered.
The garment hangs straight, without following the shape of the body.

items.d: There is no special garment. Stitched clothing is worn as usual, covering as it normally would, and the colour is not fixed. Iḥrām as a garment is a men’s matter; a woman enters iḥrām in what she would ordinarily wear.

items.t: The face is not covered by cloth resting on it

art.cap: The item on a plain display block. The brim carries the veil forward, so the cloth hangs away from whatever is beneath it.

marks.t: The cap, wrapped over the crown.
A stiffened brim reaches forward from the front edge.
The veil hangs from the outer rim of that brim.
It falls with a gap, touching nothing beneath it.

items.d: A woman in iḥrām does not cover her face in the way a niqāb rests on it. Where men are present it is covered by a screen held clear of the face — the usual arrangement is a cap or a stiffened band that carries the cloth forward so nothing touches.

A woman says it at a volume she can hear herself, where a man raises his voice. It is said just as often, and iḥrām is not complete without it: the intention and the talbiyah together are what begin it, the same for both.

Iḥrām itself is entered as usual — the ghusl, the intention and the talbiyah are not prevented. What is prevented is entering the Masjid, and ṭawāf is inside the Masjid and is farḍ, so the ʿUmrah cannot be completed until it has passed. That makes this a question to put to the ʿulamā before the flights are booked rather than after: what to do when the return date is fixed, what the position is on delaying a period, and what is owed if the group has to leave first. None of that is answered here. This entry exists so the question gets asked early enough to matter.

sections.title: What is not done in iḥrām

items.d: Scent, perfume, perfumed oil, anything with a fragrance — on the body, on the clothes, or in what you eat and drink. Including scented soap, shampoo, deodorant and some toothpaste, which is why the packing list sends people to buy unscented before flying.
Shaving or clipping hair from anywhere on the body, and cutting the nails. Hair that comes away by itself while you are washing, with no intention of removing it, is not the same thing.
Hunting a wild animal, and also helping or pointing one out to somebody else who is. It reaches further down than people expect — killing a louse falls under it.

Obscenity, transgression and argument, and harming another Muslim with a word as much as with an elbow. Not a matter of dam, but of what the Qurʾān asks of a pilgrim, and worth saying in a crowd of two million in the heat.

items.t: Shade, as long as it does not touch you
items.d: An umbrella, a parasol, the roof of a car or a coach, the shade of a wall. None of it is covering the head in the sense iḥrām means, because none of it rests on the head. In the heat this matters more than it sounds: see the heat branch.

items.t: A ring, glasses, a watch, a money belt
items.d: A ring, spectacles, a hearing aid, a wristwatch, and a belt or pouch that keeps your money and documents on you. The belt being fine is the reason one is on the packing list — stitching is not the test here, the garment is.

You may wash your body and hair, and change the sheets or wash them. Soap is the part that needs the ʿulamā to be exact — scented soap is already out under perfume, and there is more to say about plain soap than one line here can carry. The packing list sends people to buy unscented before flying for this reason.

items.t: A blanket over you at night
items.d: A blanket, a quilt or a sleeping bag over the body, feet included. The head and face are what stay clear, not the rest of you, and a cold night in Minā is not a reason to lie uncovered.
A miswāk for the teeth. Carrying something on your head is not covering it. Hair that comes away by itself while you wash, with no intention of removing it, is not cutting it.

branches.title: The rites, in order
branches.sub: What is done, when, and in what order
branches.lead: What is done, when, and in what order.

items.d: At the mīqāt or before it: ghusl if you can manage it, wuḍūʾ if you cannot, then the two sheets. Men may put ʿiṭr on now and not after. Pray two rakʿahs nafl with the head covered, then sit bareheaded, make the intention for ʿUmrah, and say the talbiyah three times — men aloud, women quietly. Iḥrām begins with the intention and the talbiyah, not with the cloth: the restrictions start from that moment. Flying from Manchester this is a decision made on the plane, because Jeddah is already past the boundary. Somebody already in Makkah goes out to Masjid Tanʿīm to enter iḥrām.

art.cap: The maṭāf from above. The arrows follow the way the circuit is walked.

marks.t: Al-Ḥajar al-Aswad, set in this corner.
The door, on the wall between that corner and the ʿIrāqī corner.
The Ḥaṭīm, the low semicircular wall, and the ground it encloses.

items.d: Before you reach the corner, stop the talbiyah, men make idṭibāʿ, and the intention is made — it has to be made before you get there. Stand level with the Black Stone, turn to face the Kaʿbah and do istilām. Then move off to your right, keep the Kaʿbah on your left, and go round it anticlockwise. Istilām again at the end of each round, seven rounds in all. The section below has the details; the one that catches people is that what must be right is where a round starts and where it ends.

Two rakʿahs at Maqām Ibrāhīm, wājib, with Sūrat al-Kāfirūn and then al-Ikhlāṣ, and duʿā after. If there is no room at the Maqām — and most of the time there is not — anywhere in the Masjid will do, and trying to force a space there is the wrong trade. Then Zamzam, facing the Kaʿbah, as much as you can take. Then the Multazam, between the Black Stone and the door, where you put your chest and arms against the wall and ask. Either order for those two. Then back to the stone for one more istilām before saʿī, which is mustaḥabb rather than required.

Out to Ṣafā, climbing until the Kaʿbah comes into view between the pillars, and make the intention there. Facing it, hands raised to the shoulders, takbīr and tahlīl three times, durūd, and then duʿā for as long as you can — this is one of the places where duʿā is answered and most people leave it too quickly. Walk to Marwa at your normal pace; between the green lights men quicken to a jog and women do not. Ṣafā to Marwa is one lap, not a return trip, so seven laps end at Marwa. Two rakʿahs afterwards are mustaḥabb.

Men either shave the head or trim it, and the trim has to take at least an inch off the whole head rather than a tidy-up at the sides. Shaving carries the greater reward. Women take a little over an inch from the end of the plait. With that the ʿUmrah is finished and everything iḥrām had closed off is open again.

No special garment — ordinary clothing that covers as it normally would, and the face left uncovered by anything resting on it. Ghusl or wuḍūʾ, the two rakʿahs, the intention and the talbiyah, the same as anyone, with the talbiyah said quietly. The iḥrām branch has the detail, including ḥayḍ and nifās, which is worth reading before booking rather than before flying.

Idṭibāʿ and ramal are both men’s Sunnahs and neither applies: no shoulder is bared and the first three rounds are walked at the same pace as the other four. Everything else is the same rite — the start and end in line with the Black Stone, the Ḥaṭīm gone round, the Kaʿbah kept on the left. Istilām from where you are standing rather than pressing into the crowd is the ordinary way it is done.

The stretch between the two sets of green lights is where men quicken to a jog. Women walk it at their own pace, the same as the rest of the mas‘ā. Seven laps ending at Marwa, and the standing duʿā at both ends, are unchanged.
The head is not shaved. A little over an inch is taken from the end of the plait, and with that iḥrām ends and its restrictions lift.

A green light on the arched wall faces the corner the Black Stone sits in, and that corner is the one facing the single minaret — the other three face two each. The strip of dark marble that used to mark the line across the floor is gone, so you judge it by eye. Nobody can be exact about it and you are not required to be.

items.t: Where a round begins and ends
items.d: This is the part that actually has to be right. A round that starts after you have already passed the stone is short, and a seventh that ends before you reach it is short. If you are unsure on the last one, keep walking until you are sure rather than stopping early.

Raise the hands to the ears with the palms towards the stone, say bismillāh and the takbīr, place both palms on it and kiss it without force. If you cannot reach it, touch it with a hand, or raise the hands towards it and kiss them. Done at the end of every round.

items.t: The stone is not worth hurting somebody for
items.d: Kissing the Black Stone is Sunnah. Not harming a Muslim is farḍ. A Sunnah is not carried out by breaking a farḍ, and pushing through a crowd to reach the stone trades the greater thing for the lesser one. When it is packed, raise your hands from where you are, say bismillāh Allāhu akbar, and keep moving with the flow.

items.t: The Ḥaṭīm is part of the Kaʿbah
items.d: The low semicircular wall on the far side encloses ground that belongs to the Kaʿbah, so the circuit passes outside it. Cutting between the wall and the building shortens the round. The plan on the ṭawāf step shows which wall it stands on.

items.t: The Kaʿbah stays on your left
items.d: All the way round. Not your back to it, not your chest, not your right shoulder — which is the usual way it happens, when somebody turns to look at it or to take a photograph and keeps walking.

Ramal is a brisk, short-stepped walk with the chest out and the shoulders moving, in the first three rounds only. Idṭibāʿ is the ridāʾ taken under the right arm and thrown over the left shoulder, leaving the right shoulder bare; it is for ṭawāf and nothing else, so it comes off once the seventh round is done — not worn to saʿī and not worn to ṣalāh.

The corner you pass just before the Black Stone. Touch it with both hands or the right hand if you can reach it; it is not kissed and the hands are not raised towards it the way they are at the stone.

There is no set duʿā for the rounds, and the printed booklets that give one for each circuit are a convenience rather than a requirement. Ask for what you actually need, in whatever language it comes in. Between the Yamānī corner and the Black Stone the Sunnah is Rabbanā ātinā, which is in the duʿās branch. Keep your voice down — the person beside you is also asking.

Ṣafā to Marwa is one. Marwa to Ṣafā is two. Counted that way the seventh finishes at Marwa, and anyone who ends back at Ṣafā has walked fourteen. The counter in this section counts it the right way round and tells you which end the next lap leaves from.
Men quicken to a jog between the two sets of green lights and walk normally either side of them. Women walk at their own pace the whole way, including between the lights.

items.t: You cannot see the Kaʿbah from Marwa
items.d: At Ṣafā you climb until it comes into view between the pillars. At Marwa it is not visible at all now, so you climb and face its direction. People stand looking for it and hold up the people behind them.

Facing the Kaʿbah, hands raised to the shoulders as in duʿā, takbīr and tahlīl three times, durūd, then ask. The same at both ends, every lap. This is the part of saʿī most people cut short, and it is the part the walking is for.

Iḥrām is entered again for the Hajj itself, with the intention and the talbiyah, and from this point the restrictions are back on. Then out to Minā, about eight kilometres from the Ḥaram, before Ẓuhr if you can manage it. Five prayers are prayed there — Ẓuhr, ʿAṣr, Maghrib, ʿIshāʾ, and Fajr the next morning — and the four-rakʿah prayers are shortened to two, each at its own time and NOT combined. The night is spent at Minā. Little is asked of you today beyond being in the right place and resting, which is the point: tomorrow is the long one.

This is the day the Hajj is. Leave Minā after sunrise and be inside the boundary of ʿArafah from past midday until sunset — the wuqūf. Miss the standing and there is no Hajj to complete; everything else on these five days can be repaired one way or another and this cannot. 

The khuṭbah is given at Masjid Namirah, and Ẓuhr and ʿAṣr are joined behind the imām there. IN THE ḤANAFĪ SCHOOL that joining is for those praying behind the imām: somebody praying in their tent prays each at its own time. Spend the afternoon facing the qiblah asking, standing if your legs will take it and sitting if they will not — it is the asking that is the rite, not the standing. 

Do not climb Jabal al-Raḥmah looking for a ritual there; there is no authentic basis for it and the level ground is where the day is meant to be spent. Leave only after the sun has set.

Maghrib is not prayed at ʿArafah and not on the road: it is prayed at Muzdalifah together with ʿIshāʾ, at ʿIshāʾ’s time, one adhān and an iqāmah for each. 

Then sleep. The Prophet ﷺ slept here until near Fajr and the night is for rest, not for standing — you will need it. Pray Fajr early and stay until just before sunrise; that standing is itself part of the Hajj. 

Pebbles are gathered here or at Minā: forty-nine if you leave on the twelfth, seventy if you stay for the thirteenth, and a few spare is sensible because they get dropped.

Back to Minā, and three things in this order: seven pebbles at Jamrat al-ʿAqabah alone with a takbīr at each, then the qurbānī, then the head shaved or clipped — men shaved or trimmed all over, women a fingertip’s length. The talbiyah stops at the first pebble. 

After the ḥalq you are out of iḥrām for everything except intimacy with your spouse, and you may wear ordinary clothes and use scent again. Then ṭawāf al-ifāḍah at the Ḥaram, with saʿī if you have not already done it, and after that everything lawful before iḥrām is lawful again. 

THE ORDER IS THE PART PEOPLE GET WRONG, and doing it out of order is a question to put to the ʿulamā rather than to settle in a tent. Note that the source this entry follows places the ḥalq on the eleventh; the order here is the one the rest of this section follows, and it is the one to check.

items.t: 11 to 13 Dhul Ḥijjah — the days of Minā
items.d:
The nights are spent at Minā. Each day after midday all three jamarāt are stoned, in order — al-Ūlā, al-Wusṭā, then al-ʿAqabah — seven pebbles each with a takbīr at every throw. Stop after the first and after the second, face the qiblah and make duʿā; there is no standing after the third. 

You may leave after stoning on the twelfth if you are out of Minā before sunset. IF SUNSET ON THE TWELFTH FINDS YOU STILL THERE the thirteenth’s stoning falls due, and what is owed if you leave anyway is a question for the ʿulamā. 

Do not throw sandals, bottles or anything else at the pillars: there is nothing in them, and the stoning is a remembrance of Ibrāhīm ﷺ refusing Iblīs, not an attack on anything.

The last thing done in Makkah: seven laps, two rakʿahs at the Maqām, and Zamzam. No saʿī after it and nothing shaved. 

IN THE ḤANAFĪ SCHOOL it is wājib for a pilgrim who came from outside the mīqāt, and what is owed for missing it is a question for the ʿulamā; the Mālikīs hold it sunnah. A woman in ḥayḍ or nifās is excused it and does not make it up. Leave Makkah after it rather than going back to shop, which is what people do and what the farewell is meant not to be.

branches.title: The duʿās
branches.lead: What is said, where, with the pronunciation to read from.

items.ar: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أُرِيدُ الْعُمْرَةَ فَيَسِّرْهَا لِي وَتَقَبَّلْهَا مِنِّي
items.tr: Allāhumma innī urīdul-ʿumrata fa-yassirhā lī wa taqabbalhā minnī
items.when: Bareheaded, after the two rakʿahs at the mīqāt
items.d: “O Allah, I intend to perform ʿUmrah. Make it easy for me and accept it from me.” Said sitting, after the two rakʿahs and with the head uncovered. The talbiyah follows it, and the two together are what begin iḥrām.

items.ar: لَبَّيْكَ اللَّهُمَّ لَبَّيْكَ، لَبَّيْكَ لَا شَرِيكَ لَكَ لَبَّيْكَ، إِنَّ الْحَمْدَ وَالنِّعْمَةَ لَكَ وَالْمُلْكَ، لَا شَرِيكَ لَكَ
items.tr: Labbayk Allāhumma labbayk, labbayka lā sharīka laka labbayk, innal-ḥamda wan-niʿmata laka wal-mulk, lā sharīka lak
items.when: Three times at the mīqāt, then as often as you can until Makkah
items.d: “Here I am at Your service, O Allah, here I am. Here I am, You have no partner, here I am. Truly all praise and favour are Yours, and the dominion. You have no partner.” Three times when iḥrām is entered, men aloud and women quietly, then kept up on the road and stopped before you reach the Black Stone to begin ṭawāf. The ʿulamā should confirm the wording against the masjid’s own source the way the app’s other duʿās are verified.

items.ar: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ وَالصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ عَلَى رَسُولِ اللَّهِ، اللَّهُمَّ افْتَحْ لِي أَبْوَابَ رَحْمَتِكَ
items.tr: Bismillāhi waṣ-ṣalātu was-salāmu ʿalā rasūlillāh. Allāhummaftaḥ lī abwāba raḥmatik
items.d: “In the name of Allah, and peace and blessings be upon the Messenger of Allah. O Allah, open for me the doors of Your mercy.”

items.t: The first time you see the Kaʿbah
items.ar: اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ، لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
items.d: “Allah is the greatest. There is no god but Allah.” Three times, then durūd, then ask — standing where you are and facing it. People walk straight past this moment towards the crowd. It is one of the places duʿā is answered, and it comes once.

items.ar: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ، اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ وَلِلَّهِ الْحَمْدُ
items.when: At the start of ṭawāf and the end of every round
items.d: “In the name of Allah, Allah is the greatest, and all praise is for Allah.” Hands raised towards the stone. In a crowd this is said from where you are standing, without pushing in.

items.ar: رَبَّنَآ اٰتِنَا فِى الدُّنْيَا حَسَنَةً وَّفِى الْاٰخِرَةِ حَسَنَةً وَّقِنَا عَذَابَ النَّارِ
items.tr: Rabbanā ātinā fid-dunyā ḥasanatan wa fil-ākhirati ḥasanatan wa qinā ʿadhāban-nār
items.when: Between the Yamānī corner and the Black Stone, every round
items.d: “Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the hereafter, and save us from the punishment of the Fire.” Al-Baqarah 201. The one stretch of ṭawāf with a Sunnah wording attached to it; the rest of the circuit has none.

items.ar: اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ، لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
items.when: Three times at each end, every lap
items.d: Facing the Kaʿbah with the hands raised to the shoulders, three times, then durūd, then duʿā — at both ends and on every lap, not only the first.

items.ar: رَبِّ اغْفِرْ وَارْحَمْ أَنْتَ الْأَعَزُّ الْأَكْرَمُ
items.when: On the way, between Ṣafā and Marwa
items.d: “My Lord, forgive and have mercy. You are the Mightiest, the Most Generous.” Nothing is fixed for the walking itself, so ask for what you need; this is the Sunnah wording to come back to between times.

branches.title: Coming home
branches.sub: Your health, and the first days back

items.t: The cough most people come back with
items.d: Dust, crowds and air conditioning. It usually settles on its own.

items.t: See a doctor if you come home feverish
items.d: And tell them you have been on Hajj or ʿUmrah. It changes what they look for, and it matters more than people realise.
People go straight back to work and then wonder why they feel wrecked for a fortnight.

items.t: Where to buy Zamzam to bring home
items.d: It is bought at the designated Zamzam counters at the airport, not packed in your own luggage from the Ḥaram. One allocation per pilgrim, and you will be asked to show a valid passport at the counter, so keep it to hand rather than in a case that has already gone through.
There are rules about how much and how it may be carried, and airlines differ. Ask your operator before you buy more than you can take.

items.t: Keeping what you came back with
items.d: Nobody can keep ʿArafah in their chest for ever, but the habits formed in those ten days are the part that can last. The masjid's own halaqah and the duʿā book in this app are the ordinary way people hold on to it.
